items.title: When externally oriented motivation appears to matter: shared and unique associations with creative-process practices and learning engagement among Chinese art students
items.abstract: Introduction Motivation is closely related to students' engagement in learning, yet the associations of intrinsic motivation (IM) and externally oriented motivation (EM) may differ depending on whether they are examined separately or simultaneously. This study examined their shared and unique associations with self-reported creative-process practices (CPP) and learning engagement (LE) among Chinese university art students. Methods Survey data were collected from 481 students enrolled in art programs in one Chinese province using purposive sampling. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to evaluate the four-factor measurement model, followed by structural equation modeling of three specifications: an IM-only model, an EM-only model, and a simultaneous IM-EM model. Results When examined separately, both IM and EM were positively associated with CPP and LE and showed significant indirect associations with LE through CPP. When modeled simultaneously, IM retained significant associations with CPP and LE, whereas the corresponding EM associations and its indirect association through CPP were smaller and no longer statistically significant. The CPP-LE association remained positive and statistically significant across all three model specifications. Discussion The findings indicate that externally oriented motivation can show meaningful associations when considered independently, but much of this association may overlap with intrinsic motivational variance. They also highlight the importance of distinguishing separate from unique motivational associations and of treating creative-process practices and learning engagement as related but conceptually distinct aspects of creative learning.

items.title: When is an LLM-as-a-Judge Good Enough?
items.abstract: Generative AI models are capable of generating human-like content, such as large language models (LLMs) generate texts. To automate processes, certain requirements regarding trustworthiness and correctness are fulfilled. To relieve people from controlling the created content, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge is available. In this scenario, another instance of an LLM is prompted to act as a judge, and check the generated content for certain quality requirements. However, such a judgement might not always align with a human judgement. Besides noise and errors in the human judgement, another reason is just the fact that different human evaluators can have different opinions about the evaluation. One reason could be that there might be no universal or unequivocal assessment since it is challenging to formulate objective rules. This natural existence of variance in human judgement defines the best possible benchmark level of alignment for a model judge. In this work, a method is presented to calculate this best possible benchmark under variance in human judgement. By comparing the distribution of the deviations between human judgement with the distribution of the deviation between model and human judgement with statistical means allows defining a model judge as good enough. Thus, a pragmatic way is provided to decide whether human judgement for a specific task can reliably be automated by a model judge in the quality that we can expect from the corresponding human judges. The code and prompts of the analysis performed are available under https://github.com/Ocean-code-1995/llm-judge-good-enough .

items.title: When Labels Lie: Dissociating Source–Scale Bias From Experienced Performance in Decision Support
items.abstract: Decision support systems (DSS) are often evaluated before users have much direct experience with them. As a result, the way these systems are labeled may shape selection, reliance, and perceived reliability from the outset. The present work examined whether displayed source and scale labels bias DSS use in a timed object-detection task. Participants searched cluttered images for a bat after choosing between advisors differentiated by source, either human-crowd or machine-generated, and scale, either medium or large. Two experiments were conducted: a default-label (DL) experiment, in which displayed labels matched the underlying recommendation source, and a flipped-label (FL) experiment, in which displayed source labels were decoupled from the underlying source. Overall, source and scale labels affected different stages of DSS use. Participants selected larger-scale labels above chance, while machine-labeled assistance was not selected more often than human-crowd-labeled assistance. Compliance was high and closely matched advisor accuracy, with slightly higher compliance for large-labeled than medium-labeled assistance. Response times mainly reflected repeated exposure. Perceived reliability ratings showed a significant label condition × displayed source interaction, and error-type analyses suggested greater vulnerability to false-positive recommendations under a human-crowd label. Together, these results suggest that source and scale labels shape initial selection, trial-level reliance, and post-use reliability judgments in different ways.

items.title: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI?
items.abstract: Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. We ask where this tendency comes from by comparing models before and after fine-tuning and by varying how questions are asked. First, pretrained models already include explicit AI/ML terms in the recommendations of 27% of their responses, and their released instruction-tuned versions do so in 59%. Second, fine-tuning models ourselves shows that this rise is not inevitable: general instruction tuning leaves the rate unchanged, but removing the 7% of instruction examples that concern AI cuts it by 14 percentage points, below the level of the pretrained models it starts from. Data rewarding helpfulness raise it by 9 points, while data ranked by the preferences of diverse simulated users lower it by 9. Finally, with models held fixed, asking for the "best" option or for what to do "right now" raises the rate by 8 and 18 points, whereas telling the model it is an AI advisor adds 4. Overall, the tendency starts in pretraining, and what models learn afterward, together with how a question is phrased, decides how strongly it appears.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Why Bother Me Again? Benchmarking Personal Agent Memory for Interaction Preferences
items.abstract: Personal intelligence systems are taking on increasingly complex everyday tasks, yet repeated questions, unnecessary confirmations, and unwanted outreach can turn capable assistance into interaction burden. Reducing this burden requires agents to remember how users want to be assisted. However, existing memory benchmarks focus on factual recall and personalized answers and rarely test how agents learn and act on interaction preferences. We introduce MemPABench, an interactive environment for on-policy evaluation of memory in personal agents. MemPABench poses long-horizon tasks requiring agents to decide when to clarify, confirm, or act autonomously. Four grounded simulated users hold 14 preferences across work and personal contexts. Their feedback spans 99 sessions over four months, with five event-driven changes per user testing memory updates. We evaluate preference selection, delivered behavior, and sensitivity to context and preference change. Evaluating four memory systems across four LLM backbones, we find that current memory brings limited gains in preference selection. Retrieval-based systems (i.e. Mem0, MemOS, simple RAG) do not outperform No Memory, while File-based memory improves accuracy but applies preferences beyond relevant contexts. Our analysis shows that current memory struggles to retrieve interaction preferences and adapt to preference changes. Even with the correct preference available, overriding the agent's default interaction habits remains challenging. The environment and dataset are available at https://mempabench.com.

items.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
items.abstract: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

items.title: With a Little Help From AI?! Governing Visual Hate Speech Through AI-Assisted Counter-Image Practices
items.abstract: The attention-grabbing and memorable nature of visuals makes them a powerful vehicle for spreading hate online. As platforms increasingly reconsider or scale back content moderation efforts, user-centered interventions are gaining importance as complementary governance strategies. While prior research demonstrates the effectiveness of empathy-based textual counter speech, little is known about the role of visual counter speech in mitigating hateful imagery. This preregistered study examines the effectiveness of user-centered interventions against visual hate speech. Using an experimental design (N = 666), we tested four interventions against a no-intervention control condition in response to hateful images targeting transgender persons: (a) empathy-based textual counter speech, (b) AI-generated generic counter images, (c) AI-generated specific counter images replicating elements of the original, and (d) platform-issued warning labels. Results show substantial variation across interventions. Empathy-based textual counter speech and AI-generated specific counter images showed the most consistent reductions in amplification-oriented behaviors, particularly forwarding. Visual interventions did not outperform textual counter speech, suggesting that effectiveness depends less on modality and more on the specificity and contextual alignment of the intervention. Furthermore, effectiveness varied with the intensity of the hate content. Interventions were most effective for humor-based, more ambiguously harmful content, whereas their impact diminished for more severe forms of hate. The consistent performance of AI-generated specific counter images further points to the potential of generative AI to provide users with a rapid, low-cost, and accessible means of producing context-sensitive counter speech.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Work-Study Integration: A Dual-Assurance Framework for Rwandan Higher Education
items.abstract: Employment can finance higher education and generate substantial learning, yet it can also displace study, restrict scholarly participation and expose students to conflicting institutional demands. These different relationships cannot be governed adequately through a single rule on attendance or work experience. This article develops the Rwanda Integrated Work-Study Framework through a structured critical synthesis of regulatory documents, selected institutional provisions, international policy mechanisms and academic literature. A bounded, reproducibly documented search of two academic discovery services returned 50 records; after deduplication and screening, 33 reports were sought and 12 full reports were assessed and retained. Purposefully selected theoretical, policy and recent synthesis sources complemented this corpus. PRISMA-informed reporting records the executed search without claiming an exhaustive systematic review. The analysis identifies a need to distinguish qualification levels, credit volume, approved duration, delivery arrangements and the assessment of workplace learning. Its central contribution is dual assurance: educational support should respond to demonstrated need, whereas academic recognition should depend on independently assessed learning. Regulatory authority and learner protection govern both decisions; credit additionally requires qualification-level equivalence. Six interconnected domains operationalise this distinction across undergraduate, master's and doctoral education. Hypothetical cases expose potential failures involving informal employment, financial hardship, clinical practice and employer-controlled research. The framework offers transparent decision rules, safeguards and evaluation measures rather than evidence of implementation effectiveness. It provides a context-sensitive basis for improving access and recognising workplace learning while retaining academic independence and demanding qualification standards.

items.title: Workplace Learning in Clinical Laboratories: Health Professionals’ Perceptions and Practices of Training Students
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction Clinical placements, where students learn through participation in everyday work, are a central component of many health education programs, including biomedical laboratory science (BLS). While research has primarily focused on students’ experiences, less is known about how participating staff perceive their role. This study explores how BLS staff perceive and enact clinical training. Materials and methods A qualitative study was conducted comprising four focus groups with BLS staff from two hospital settings, including both experienced and newly employed staff. Interviews were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Activity theory guided a subsequent analysis of workplace learning tensions. Results Six themes were identified, reflecting staff perceptions related to student training: (1) professional pride and ambassador for the field, (2) organisational aspects, (3) interpretations and perceptions of student motivation and engagement, (4) aspects of own motivation and engagement, (5) responses to perceived student engagement and methods to engage students, and (6) confidence in students, students as helpers. Staff expressed a positive commitment to supporting students and fostering professional identity. However, an Activity Theory analysis identified five interconnected tensions related to production, laboratory quality, onboarding of newly hired, division of responsibility, and pedagogical resources. These tensions shaped staffs’ opportunities to involve and support students in clinical work. Discussion Side-by-side training is an integrated and often implicit part of everyday work. Strengthening clinical education requires recognising training as a shared organisational responsibility and creating conditions that support student participation.

items.title: WRDO: Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization in Aligned Language Models
items.abstract: Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations.

items.title: WSM-Aware HRI: An IoT-Enhanced Framework for Early Detection and Norm-Guided Repair of Failures with LLM Guidance
items.abstract: Human–robot interaction (HRI) failures remain a major barrier to deploying robots in real-world environments. Prior work often treats failures as isolated technical faults or focuses on post-hoc recovery behaviors. In practice, many breakdowns arise because humans and robots operate under inconsistent assumptions about the current world state. We propose WSM-Aware HRI, an IoT-enhanced modular framework that unifies diverse HRI breakdowns as World-State Mismatches (WSMs) between a human's instruction-implied assumptions and a robot's grounded world model built from multimodal perception and digital augmentation. A Large Language Model (LLM) is used to make implicit assumptions explicit, map them to a small set of mismatch types, and specify the evidence needed for verification against the robot's world state. WSM-Aware HRI shifts failure handling from execution-time recovery to proactive mismatch detection during intention formation, enabling interventions guided by safety, norm compliance, and multi-user coordination with transparent explanations. We evaluate mismatch identification in ten everyday cases spanning both visual and latent-state mismatches. The system can accurately produce the expected output results, and ablations show that reliable identification depends on appropriate grounding representations and verification-oriented refinement. These results indicate that treating interaction breakdowns as explicit world–state mismatches enables earlier detection of impending failures and offers a principled mechanism for integrating external evidence and social constraints into human–robot interaction.

items.title: Yield and Yield Components in Soybean Using Genome-Wide Association Studies, GWAS: Current Status, Challenges, and Breeding Prospects
items.abstract: Molecular-genetic analysis of soybean yield and yield components under drought is a crucial element for the development of effective breeding strategies and sustainable agricultural production. The aim of this review is to critically analyse current data from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and identified genetic loci, SNP markers, and candidate genes associated with yield components in soybean in dry conditions with limited water supply and adequate watering (controls). In the results, 346 genetic associations, and 229 candidate genes with KEGG-based potential functions were sufficiently described in published papers and selected for the current study. Three statistically significant metabolic pathways were identified with isoflavonoid biosynthesis, glycosaminoglycan degradation and cysteine and methionine metabolism. The main limitation of the presented analysis was found in the low level of heritability for the studied traits, together with human factors such as carrying out and interpreting GWAS affecting the results presented in the current study. Additionally, complex multigenic controls were reported for the studied traits in soybean and a high level of genotype × environment interactions. Nevertheless, the presented data provide a basis for developing molecular strategies to improve soybean yield in conjunction with better potential drought tolerance.

items.title: YingLan: A Multimodal Ocean Foundation Model for Unified Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Observations
items.abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure. In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters, YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, corresponding to relative error reductions of 0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa, XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively. These results provide initial evidence of the model's effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations remain necessary to assess its generalization capabilities.

items.title: ZeroTrust-MapAI: A Zero-Trust Intrusion Detection Framework for Big Data Wireless Sensor Networks
items.abstract: Abstract Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are critical infrastructure yet face escalating cyber-physical threats. Traditional intrusion detection systems rely on centralized architectures and implicit trust, which become vulnerabilities in large-scale, adversarial settings. We introduce ZeroTrust-MapAI, a framework that synergizes zero-trust principles, artificial intelligence, and MapReduce to achieve secure and scalable intrusion detection for big-data WSNs. The framework continuously verifies every node and communication, employs distributed autoencoders with Byzantine-robust federated learning, and processes security logs in a MapReduce pipeline. Evaluation on two large-scale datasets yields weighted F1-scores of 0.847 on WSN-DS and 0.826 on EdgeIIoTset, outperforming standard baselines. Under 30% Byzantine attack, ZeroTrust-MapAI maintains strong performance (F1: 0.829– 0.841 across attack types), while FedAvg degrades significantly. The MapReduce pipeline demonstrates effective parallelization with nearlinear speedup up to 8 partitions. This work provides a practical architectural blueprint for building secure, scalable, zero-trust-inspired sensing infrastructures.

items.title: "Artificial Intelligence in Banking Fraud Detection: A Systematic Review using the Prisma Approach"
items.abstract: The rapid growth of digital banking, instant payments, mobile applications and card-not-present transactions has improved access to financial services while simultaneously widening the attack surface for fraud.Conventional rulebased systems remain indispensable for regulatory control, yet they are often unable to recognize subtle, coordinated and previously unseen patterns.This paper presents a condensed systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) in banking fraud detection, organised according to the PRISMA 2020 reporting logic.It synthesizes evidence on supervised learning, anomaly detection, deep learning, graph analytics, natural language processing and hybrid decision systems.The review shows that tree-based ensembles generally perform strongly on structured transaction data; sequential neural networks are useful for behavioural histories; graph methods are promising for mule-account and fraud-ring detection; and anomaly models support discovery where labels are scarce.However, accuracy alone is misleading in highly imbalanced datasets.Precision, recall, F1-score, precision-recall area, false-positive cost, detection latency and financial value saved are more meaningful.The review further identifies concept drift, delayed labels, data leakage, limited public datasets, explainability, privacy and bias as major implementation concerns.It concludes that the most credible banking architecture is layered, adaptive and human-supervised rather than dependent on a single algorithm.PRISMA 2020 is used as the reporting framework because it improves transparency in identification, screening, eligibility assessment and synthesis of studies.

items.title: “Eyes on the Network” – Task Complexity and Expertise Shape Visual Strategies and Mental Workload in Rail Traffic Control
items.abstract: ObjectiveEvaluate the sensitivity of eye-tracking metrics to variations in mental workload in rail traffic control, and how they may be modulated by operator experience.BackgroundRail traffic control is a safety-critical domain characterized by high cognitive demands. While subjective workload measures are widely used, objective, real-time indicators, particularly eye-tracking metrics, remain underexplored.MethodEighteen professional rail traffic controllers (9 novice, 9 experienced) performed a simulation-based experiment involving four different scenarios with varying traffic density and task complexity, while wearing a head-mounted eye tracker. Measures of gaze behavior and visual strategies (fixations in different areas of interest (AOI)) were computed, and compared to subjective workload measures, to assess the effects of task difficulty and experience.ResultsSome measures like pupil dilation showed substantial changes (by ∼100%), while others like stationary gaze entropy showed more modest changes (∼40%), with increased task demand. Measures such as fixation rate revealed significant interaction effects with experience, indicating distinct visual strategies of novices vs. experts. Compared to experts, novices relied more on global overview displays under higher workload, and reduced planning-related information use, as revealed by AOI analysis. Subjective workload measures corroborated with increases in perceived demand.ConclusionThis study advances mental workload assessment in rail traffic control by demonstrating that eye-tracking metrics are sensitive to workload variations, and also reveal underlying cognitive strategies unique to expertise.ApplicationThese findings support the development of real-time workload monitoring systems and inform training interventions focused on information integration and cognitive strategies in rail traffic control operations.

items.title: "From Access to Empowerment: Technology as a Transformative Infrastructure in Inclusive Heritage Tourism"
items.abstract: Heritage tourism is at a critical inflection point. While access infrastructure has improved considerably over the past two decades, a persistent gap remains between physical access and meaningful participation for visitors with disabilities. This chapter argues that the challenge of inclusive heritage tourism is no longer primarily one of quantity, such as ramps, captioning, or barrier-free entry points, but of quality: of experience, agency, and empowerment. Drawing on a sociotechnical perspective and grounded in the social model of disability, the chapter proposes a three-tiered conceptual framework moving from Access to Inclusion to Empowerment, and examines the role of intelligent, adaptive, and participatory technologies as the infrastructure that can bridge these tiers. Four technology domains are examined in depth: User-governed journey orchestration systems, user-controlled AI travel companions, adaptive multisensory and extended reality (XR) platforms, and co-creative generative AI heritage applications. The chapter concludes with implications for heritage managers, technology developers, and policymakers, and charts a future research agenda centred on governance, dignity, and co-design.

items.title: “It feels like hard work trying to talk to it”: Understanding How Older Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) Experience and Repair Interactional and Conversational Breakdowns with Voice Assistants (VAs)
items.abstract: Designing Conversational AI systems to support older adults with MCI necessitates robustness in handling complex and personalized interactions. In this study, we investigate how older adults with MCI experience, navigate and attempt to repair breakdowns while interacting with a voice-based AI system in their homes for medication management through the lens of interactional ”seams”. Through a 20-week in-home deployment with 7 participant dyads, we analyzed 844 interactions to identify interactional and conversational breakdowns and user repair strategies. Drawing on post-deployment interviews, we reflect on the nature of these breakdowns and older adults’ experiences of mitigating them. We further illustrate how older adults draw on their situated knowledge and environment to make sense of and recover from these disruptions, highlighting the cognitive effort required in doing so. Our findings emphasize the collaborative nature of interaction in human-AI contexts, and point to the need for voice assistants to better align with users’ expectations for memory, their routines and external resources in their environment. We conclude by discussing opportunities for voice assistants to integrate contextual knowledge from older adults’ sociotechnical environment and to facilitate more meaningful and user-centered interactions.

items.title: A Digital Twin to Improve Cyber-Social Impact
items.abstract: The increasing complexity of Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and their integration with IT infrastructures has significantly expanded the cyber threat landscape. Traditional cybersecurity models, primarily based on the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA triad), fail to capture the broader societal and operational impacts of cyberattacks. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Digital Twin technology with a Cyber-Social Security model to simulate, analyze, and quantify cyber threats in critical infrastructures. Virtualized ICS environments built with Mininet and MiniCPS are used to model attack scenarios and assess their consequences across technical and social dimensions. At the core of the framework lies the Cyber-Social Vulnerability Scoring System (CSVSS), a quantitative metric that extends CVSS with a Social Impact dimension grounded in the Entity and Place pillars, producing a single, reproducible severity score that reflects real-world consequences. Crucially, the framework does not automate risk assessment but keeps the human analyst at its center: a Large Language Model (LLM) performs a first-pass analysis, mapping vulnerabilities and drafting risk reports, while the analyst, supported by explainable AI feedback, validates the findings and retains decision authority over critical cases. Experimental results demonstrate the framework's ability to model and score cyber-social impact, while the human-in-the-loop design is presented as a conceptual principle to preserve oversight.

items.title: A High Fidelity Simulation Study in Assessing Proficiency of Emergency Medical Professionals in Prehospital Management of Traumatic Hemorrhagic Shock
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction: According to the World Health Organization, traffic accidents are a leading cause of fatalities, particularly among young adults aged 5–29, with hemorrhage being the primary cause of death in traumatic incidents. The average time from the onset of shock to death is approximately 2 h, illustrating the need for rapid assessment, timely intervention, and prompt transport to a trauma centre. EEmergency Medical Professional (EMP), are typically the first on the scene to attend to patients with traumatic injuries and play a crucial role in determining patient outcomes; they must be on their toes in the management of these emergencies. Methods: Our aim was to assess the proficiency of Emergency Medical Professionals (EMPs) in handling hemorrhagic shock in a simulated scenario. The simulation study comprised 300 Emergency Medical Professionals, both new and experienced across India, and was conducted over a period of 6 months. The participants were scored on a checklist with a maximum of 10 points. High-fidelity manikins were used, and participants were divided into 30 groups for 45-min sessions, which included pre-briefing, simulation, and debriefing. Results: The results demonstrate strong proficiency among EMPs in initial trauma assessment skills but reveal critical gaps in recognizing life-threatening conditions like exsanguinating hemorrhage and “Load and Go” situations. Despite exhibiting technical proficiency in the International Trauma Life Support ITLS primary survey, participants struggled to translate assessments into life-saving interventions. There was a significant failure to recognize exsanguinating hemorrhage (46.7%), declare “load-and-go” situations (36.3%), and administer tranexamic acid (0%). In the Indian context of prolonged transport times, this lack of situational awareness is concerning. Bridging this gap requires targeted, simulation-based experiential learning to help EMPs evolve from simply completing checklists to executing rapid, critical prioritization in real-world emergencies. Conclusion: The study highlights a notable proficiency gap among EMPs in key shock management skills, emphasizing the importance of continuous training to enhance patient outcomes and elevate care standards in trauma care.

items.title: A machine learning model for early warning of treatment failure in autoimmune hepatitis: a 10-year real-world study
items.abstract: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) can progress rapidly to end-stage liver disease without timely remission. Interpatient heterogeneity and severe presentations often preclude standard immunosuppression, increasing early clinical deterioration in hospitalized patients even with standard care. We developed and independently validated a machine-learning model to predict treatment failure risk upon admission. We conducted a dual-cohort study comprising a retrospective discovery cohort (n = 314, 2017–2025) and a consecutive temporal validation cohort (n = 66, 2025–2026). Following ensemble-based feature selection, 13 machine-learning algorithms were evaluated. The optimal model was interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and benchmarked against the conventional Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) and Child-Pugh score. Seven predictors were identified: alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total bile acid (TBA), Child-Pugh score, immunoglobulin M (IgM), total bilirubin (TBil), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). The Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM) achieved superior discrimination (AUC = 0.762), significantly outperforming MELD (AUC = 0.555) and Child-Pugh (AUC = 0.611) scores, with satisfactory calibration and clinical utility. Predictive efficacy was maintained in the temporal validation cohort (AUC = 0.755). SHAP analysis revealed a dual biological trade-off: pronounced inflammatory activity (elevated ALT) inversely correlated with treatment failure risk, whereas severe cholestasis and impaired hepatic reserve drove adverse outcomes. This non-invasive GBM model quantifies the complex clinical interplay among active inflammation, cholestatic severity, and depleted hepatic reserve. Overcoming limitations of static scoring systems, it provides a reliable, actionable tool for personalized risk stratification and preemptive therapeutic decision-making in heterogeneous AIH patients upon index admission. When patients are hospitalized for autoimmune hepatitis, it is often difficult for doctors to predict who will worsen despite receiving standard treatments. We developed an artificial intelligence tool that uses routine blood tests to calculate a patient’s risk of treatment failure the moment they are admitted to the hospital. This early warning system allows doctors to quickly identify high-risk patients and personalize their care with more effective or intensive therapies right from the start.

items.title: A Manifesto for the Age of Autonomous AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence moves beyond answering questions and begins acting on our behalf, institutions face two connected problems. People may retain formal authority while losing the practical conditions needed to exercise judgment. Meanwhile, AI systems can carry out technically correct actions without legitimate authorization. This manifesto argues for human agency, legitimate institutional authority, and accountable action. It examines meaningful human oversight, the limits of delegated authority, verification when actions produce consequences, and the obligations of those who govern AI. Its guiding principle, Authority Before Autonomy, calls for responsible delegation without surrendering the capacity to question, correct, and answer for what follows.

items.title: A Review on Matrix Tablet for Sustained Drug Release
items.abstract: The oral route remains the most preferred route for drug administration due to its ease and patient acceptance, but conventional dosage forms require frequent dosing which leads to fluctuations in plasma drug levels. To overcome this problem, sustained release matrix tablets have been developed as an effective alternative. In this system, the drug is uniformly dispersed within a polymer matrix that controls its release over an extended period of time. Various types of polymers such as hydrophilic polymers like hydroxypropyl methylcellulose, hydrophobic polymers like ethyl cellulose and natural polymers like xanthan gum and guar gum are used as release retardants. The release of drug from matrix tablet takes place mainly by diffusion through gel layer, swelling of polymer and slow erosion of matrix. Recently, the field has witnessed remarkable innovations including blending of natural and synthetic polymers, introduction of gastro-retentive and mucoadhesive matrix systems, application of 3D printing for personalized tablets and development of pH sensitive smart matrices. These advancements have improved the efficiency and safety of matrix systems. Looking ahead, the combination of biodegradable polymers, nanocarriers and artificial intelligence based design is expected to make matrix tablets more targeted, sustainable and patient friendly. This review summarizes the current status, release mechanisms, recent developments and future scope of matrix tablets for sustained drug delivery.

items.title: A Shared-Task-State-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Knowledge Graph Construction in Substation Operation and Maintenance
items.abstract: Knowledge graph construction typically involves data preprocessing, entity recognition, relation extraction, knowledge fusion, conflict resolution, and quality assessment. However, heterogeneous documents in substation operation and maintenance (O&M), including technical standards, defect records, work tickets, operational logs, and scanned or mixed-format documents, exhibit dense domain terminology, inconsistent expressions, cross-source conflicts, and incomplete provenance, which make accurate and traceable knowledge construction challenging. Existing large-language-model-based and pipeline-based methods have improved automatic knowledge extraction, but their processing stages are usually weakly coupled, making it difficult to reuse cross-stage evidence, trace downstream errors to responsible upstream tasks, and perform targeted rework. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a shared-task-state-driven multi-agent collaborative knowledge graph construction framework (MAC-CKG). The framework introduces a task orchestrator and a shared task-state pool to coordinate five agents for data processing, entity recognition, relation extraction, knowledge fusion, and quality assessment; provenance, confidence, conflict, and review information are preserved across stages, while ontology constraints, multifactor confidence, and the two-threshold quality-routing mechanism jointly support knowledge insertion, human review, and targeted rework. For evaluation, we constructed a heterogeneous substation O&M dataset comprising 96 heterogeneous source items (including documents and structured knowledge resources) and 17,220 standardized input units, yielding a provenance-verified candidate subset of 9519 entities and 9258 relations. An independently annotated 20-document end-to-end benchmark was separately used for raw-document extraction evaluation. Across three independent runs on this benchmark, MAC-CKG achieves mean entity, conditional relation, and strict triple F1 scores of 85.96%, 62.50%, and 62.31%, respectively, outperforming SAC-KG by 2.83, 5.77, and 6.34 percentage points and PiVe by 4.48, 8.32, and 8.94 percentage points. Independent-benchmark ablation further reduces triple F1 from 62.31% to 59.68% without task orchestration and to 57.41% without the shared task-state pool, showing sensitivity to these components under the evaluated configurations, with inference cost considered separately.

items.title: A Study on The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Human Resource Management
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for Human Resource Management (HRM), including recruitment, employee selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, and workforce planning. This paper reviews the applications, potential benefits, challenges, and ethical considerations associated with AI in HRM. The study follows a descriptive approach based on secondary sources, including academic literature and professional reports. The review suggests that AI may support routine tasks, organize workforce information, and assist HR decisionmaking. However, privacy, algorithmic bias, implementation costs, accuracy, technical knowledge, and employee trust remain important concerns. The paper concludes that AI should support rather than replace human judgement, with responsible policies, data protection, and appropriate human supervision.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Class-Aware and Class-Agnostic CNN Attribution via Spectral Mapping and Confidence-Adaptive Fusion
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has historically diverged into class-aware methods, which highlight discriminative regions for specific target classes, and class-agnostic methods, which capture dominant feature representations regardless of the classification outcome. In this paper, we introduce a unified attribution framework that bridges this gap by explicitly separating the attribution target from the feature extraction operator. Specifically, we project deep activations onto multiple dominant principal components to extract robust, class-agnostic structural maps, while utilizing class-aware gradients to localize target-specific semantics. To synthesize these complementary perspectives, we propose a logit-margin-based fusion mechanism that shifts attribution priority based on the model’s predictive margin. We evaluate our framework in a cross-domain zero-shot setting by applying ImageNet-pretrained architectures (ResNet-50, DenseNet-121) to the Oxford-IIIT Pet dataset. Our zero-shot evaluation shows that the proposed fusion provides an alternative combination of class-aware and class-agnostic evidence. The results suggest that adaptively combining feature-level representation maps with target-driven discriminative maps offers a distinct tool for interpreting CNN representations across domain shifts.

items.title: A world in chaos: Who engineers, amplifies and exploits crisis on the road to 2030?
items.abstract: This documentary essay examines how political, military, environmental, and public-health crises are deliberately produced, amplified, or exploited, and how their consequences may shape governance on the road to 2030. Drawing on institutional records, declassified archives, scientific and humanitarian assessments, contemporary reporting, and the author’s earlier writings, it analyses developments from June 2025 to 20 October 2026 through a critical historical and biblical lens. Cases involving political unrest, Ukraine, Sudan, the Israel–Iran confrontation, natural hazards, and disease emergencies reveal distinct but interacting pathways of intentional harm, institutional opportunism, and social vulnerability. Historical records of covert intervention establish that certain forms of manipulation are real; they do not substantiate a single hidden command directing every contemporary disaster. Public agendas for international coordination, digital identity, artificial intelligence, and financial interoperability likewise create opportunities for cooperation alongside risks of surveillance, exclusion, and concentrated power. The essay evaluates the unverified letter attributed to Albert Pike, the biblical accounts of Isaac and Ishmael, and Persia’s appearance in Ezekiel 38–39 without equating contested claims or eschatological interpretations with historical proof. It also considers military adaptation during the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts while distinguishing operational learning from a predetermined world-war strategy. Retrospective comparison with the author’s pre-2025 warnings identifies thematic continuities but no verified prophetic timetable. A four-part framework distinguishes direct orchestration, organized amplification, opportunistic exploitation, and structural convergence. The essay concludes that Christian preparedness requires biblical fidelity, evidence-based discernment, institutional accountability, compassion for victims, and watchfulness without date-setting.

items.title: A Zero-Shot Multimodal Agent Framework for Power Line Inspection via Large Language Models
items.abstract: With the widespread deployment of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart grids, visual inspection based on deep learning has significantly advanced. However, conventional object detection paradigms heavily rely on massive, high-quality annotated datasets, struggling with poor generalization and a fundamental “data-hungry” dilemma caused by the extreme scarcity of long-tail defect samples. To overcome these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel zero-shot multimodal agent framework driven by large language models (LLMs). Adopting a centralized star topology, the architecture strictly decouples physical visual perception from high-level business cognition, utilizing an LLM as the cognitive hub and a vision-language model (VLM) as the perception tool. Crucially, the system introduces a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism to dynamically align visual findings with authoritative grid regulations, supporting rule-referenced report generation. Experimental results demonstrate that, without any domain-specific fine-tuning, the proposed framework reduces false alarms under the tested configuration, with a detection F1 score of 82.52%. In a common-report comparison repeated three times, the framework achieves 65.30% correct reference-clause coverage, compared with 43.84% for a direct Qwen-VL-Max call supplied with the same visual priors and rules. The framework extends visual detection to structured, human-readable reports linked to supplied industrial rules; its grading accuracy and repeatability remain dependent on the visual observations and subsequent tool execution.

items.title: Academic integrity and artificial intelligence in initial teacher education: a documentary audit of teaching guides in Spanish universities
items.abstract: Purpose Universities are increasingly adopting institutional policies on academic integrity (AcI) and artificial intelligence (AI), but it remains unclear whether these expectations are translated coherently into the course-level documents that govern students’ learning and assessment. This article therefore examines how AcI and AI, including generative AI (GenAI), are articulated in official teaching guides for Spain’s Master’s Degree in Teacher Training, and whether guidance is embedded coherently across course design. Design/methodology/approach A documentary content analysis was conducted on 254 publicly available guides from 68 universities. Explicit AcI and AI references were coded across objectives, competencies, learning outcomes, activities and assessment. Two formative diagnostic indices measured breadth of coverage across these five sections. Mann–Whitney tests compared university and subject types; 25% of the corpus was independently double-coded. Findings AcI was mentioned in 53.5% of guides but was concentrated in assessment and competencies; 46.5% contained no valid reference. Explicit AI guidance remained marginal (6.3%) and primarily assessment-centred. Private universities showed slightly broader AcI coverage, public universities slightly broader AI coverage and Final Master’s Project guides substantially broader AcI coverage. Research limitations/implications The indices measure documentary breadth, not the quality, depth or implementation of guidance, and guides are nested within universities. Practical implications Programme leaders should integrate task-specific integrity and AI expectations across outcomes, activities, assessment, disclosure and formative support, with attention to future teachers’ professional AI literacy. Originality/value The study provides a large-scale, programme-specific audit and a transparent method for benchmarking cross-sectional curricular integration without treating document coverage as a quality score.

items.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
items.abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .

items.title: AdaptMIL: Domain Adaptation for Multiple Instance Learning in Digital Pathology
items.abstract: Pathology foundation models (PFMs) support a wide range of histopathology tasks on whole-slide images through multiple instance learning (MIL). Despite recent progress, these models remain sensitive to cross-hospital distribution shifts: performance often degrades when a task head (e.g., classification) is trained on data from one hospital and then used on data from another hospital. To address this challenge, we propose AdaptMIL, a training strategy for integrating domain adaptation into MIL training. AdaptMIL is motivated by our finding that directly applying domain adaptation objectives during MIL training can interfere with MIL aggregation learning, often resulting in performance degradation over standard training. AdaptMIL resolves this by decoupling representation-level domain alignment learning from MIL aggregation learning through a two-stage training procedure. We show that AdaptMIL improves cross-hospital performance and outperforms alternative adaptation methods across experiments spanning multiple WSI datasets, tasks, PFMs, MIL architectures, and domain adaptation objectives. AdaptMIL's code will be released upon publication.

items.title: Advances in machine learning and deep learning for antimicrobial resistance prediction
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major public health risk. Testing antimicrobial susceptibility in patients using conventional methods takes a week or more to deliver results, advances in artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL), have created an opportunity to predict AMR with speed by combining data from different sources such as genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, phenotypic, and clinical information. Recent advances in whole genome sequencing, metagenomic methods, and MALDI-TOF mass spectroscopy, as well as the availability of established and curated databases such as the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), are essential components of developing robust models for predicting AMR. A large number of studies using ML and DL methods have demonstrated that they can identify resistance genes, discover new AMR determinants, predict trends in AMR, and improve antimicrobial stewardship and drug discovery. This review describes methodologies currently used to predict AMR with a focus on the types of data used, feature engineering methods, and algorithms used in pathogen-specific and pan-species studies. It discusses several current challenges associated with building predictive models including lack of diversity of datasets, class imbalance, inconsistent methods of testing, limited ability to interpret results, and the need for further validation. Future directions involve developing explainable AI models, federated learning approaches to improve datasets, and integrating digital diagnostics into electronic health records. In conclusion, ML and DL have the potential to revolutionize precision medicine, enhance AMR monitoring, and accelerate the pace of drug development.

items.title: Advancing gender equity and inclusive digital futures through responsible agentic artificial intelligence governance
items.abstract: The shift to agentic AI represents a major paradigm change in the field of intelligent systems research and development, as these systems are capable of establishing sub-goals, planning for a goal, and executing plans with only minimal human oversight. This capability offers a unique chance to promote gender equality, inclusive digital engagement, and sustainable growth via evolving, accessible and fair AI-based methods throughout industries. Meanwhile, the increased autonomy of agentic AI systems presents unique challenges such as the potential for algorithmic bias to be amplified, decision-making disparities, and a lack of governance, each of which requires responsible AI, transparent governance, and clear ethical frameworks. This paper presents a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of a 41 paper corpus from Scopus. The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and summarizes the evidence regarding agentic and generative AI architectures, typologies of bias, and sectoral applications in healthcare, education, and gender equity. The paper presents a human-centred conceptual framework for responsible governance of agentic AI, building on lifecycle-governance and equity-by-design approaches, which merges bias mitigation, gender-inclusive design, and sustainability transition. The network of co-authorship is highly fragmented (density = 0.021; number of components = 37 from 88 authors), suggesting that there is no coordinated research agenda and giving empirical support to the integrative framework proposed here. This fragmentation further indicates that the vision and capabilities of agentic AI to contribute to gender equality and education are still not fully explored in the context of governance and sustainability, highlighting the relevance of the framework introduced in this paper. items.title: Afrofuturism is Now: Chronicling the Twenty-Year Evolution of Virtual Harlem
items.abstract: The Virtual Harlem Project (VHP) stands as a pioneering endeavor within the field of digital humanities, offering a unique opportunity to immerse oneself in the cultural and historical legacy of the Harlem Renaissance. The project originally intertwined rhetoric, history, and immersion technology to recreate Harlem in the 1920s and 1930s. It aimed to recreate the experience of Harlem life, a period marked by an explosion of African American urbanity, artistic expression, intellectualism, and social activism. Early development began in the late 1990s with the multiplayer virtual world, Second Life , but has since evolved to incorporate interactive artificial intelligence in a virtual world. In sum, the project allows participants to enter a recreated Harlem virtual world and converse with interactive figures.

items.title: After the Attacker Leaves: Benchmarking Carryover Attacks on LLM Agents
items.abstract: Modern LLM agents persist state across sessions via two channels: long-lived memory files silently prepended to the system prompt, and scheduled tasks waking the agent without user input. A one-time indirect prompt injection committed to either channel can re-fire across sessions long after the attacker leaves, threats we term carryover attacks. Existing prompt-injection benchmarks evaluate attacks only in the session where malicious content is first observed, leaving the gate governing when and how often a planted payload later re-fires unmeasured. We present CarryoverBench: 12 personal-assistant scenarios and 101 attack tasks across three trigger channels: Instant, same-turn IPI; Autonomous, heartbeat-scheduled; and Latent, memory-resurfaced. A rule-based verifier scores planting and triggering as independent stages. Across five frontier models, planted payloads re-fire without measurable decay over five rounds; conditional on successful planting, the trigger stage often provides little additional protection. Porting the Latent channel to a second runtime, Hermes, attenuates but does not eliminate the effect, suggesting that carryover defense requires runtime-layer controls in addition to prompt-level interventions.

items.title: AgenTest: Mining Business Rules to Test LLM Agents for Business Logic Bugs
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute business operations through tools and interact directly with application data and services. Beyond completing user requests, these agents must obey domain-specific business rules that constrain when actions are permitted and what data or resources may be affected. Violating such rules can lead to business logic bugs, even when a task appears successful. Detecting these bugs is difficult because the rules are rarely available as explicit, testable specifications. They are distributed across system prompts and tool definitions, while others remain implicit in domain knowledge. Existing agent testing approaches typically evaluate task success, predefined policies, or known attack scenarios. This limits their ability to systematically uncover previously unspecified business-rule violations. We present AgenTest, which mines business rules from system prompts, tool definitions, and domain knowledge, refines them into Given-When-Then specifications, and systematically tests each specification. For each extracted specification, AgenTest instantiates its Given conditions by constructing a satisfying environment state and simulated user, exercises the agent through multi-turn interactions, and checks its Then conditions over messages, tool calls, and state changes using a hybrid oracle. On the airline, retail, and telecom agents of tau2-bench with two underlying models, AgenTest produces 551 refined specifications, and detects violations of 89 and 121 distinct specifications, respectively -- 3.4X and 2.5X as many as all baselines combined. Only AgenTest detects cases where an agent improperly accesses or modifies another user's data. Moreover, about 60% of bug-triggering runs cannot be detected from the final state alone, highlighting the need to check the full interaction against explicit business rules.

items.title: AI Agents in Sports Science
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the concept of intelligent agents as a key paradigm in contemporary Artificial Intelligence and examines their applications in Sports Science and related domains. Intelligent agents are defined as autonomous, goal-oriented systems capable of perceiving their environment, reasoning over complex information, and executing context-dependent actions. The chapter distinguishes agentic systems from traditional automation, emphasizing their ability to dynamically adapt decisions based on real-time data, historical context, and evolving objectives. The chapter presents the core architectural components of intelligent agents, including the Brain, Memory, and Tools framework, and explains how these elements enable reasoning, contextual awareness, and interaction with external systems. It further explores different typologies of agentic systems, including single-agent and multi-agent architectures, and discusses the importance of guardrails, security mechanisms, and human-in-the-loop control for safe deployment. Beyond theoretical foundations, the chapter highlights practical applications in sports analytics, including training optimization, injury prevention, and personalized nutrition, as well as broader implications in higher education through adaptive learning systems and conversational agents. Through an applied case study, the chapter demonstrates how agentic AI systems can integrate multimodal data streams to support context-aware decision-making. Overall, intelligent agents are positioned as a transformative technology enabling more proactive, adaptive, and data-driven approaches in Sports Science.

items.title: AI Detection and Academic Report Analysis
items.abstract: The primary objective of this project is to determine whether the validity of written coursework as an indicator of individual skill acquisition has changed across cohorts spanning the broad availability of generative AI in research methods in the social sciences (Psychology, Pedagogics). To this end, a data processing pipeline will evaluate pseudonymized student-written research reports from the course Research Methods 2 (BA level) across five academic years: 2021-2022, 2022-2023, 2023-2024, 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 using an AI detection platform (i.e. Pangram). By breaking down research report submissions into isolated, verified academic sections (Abstract, Introduction, Method, Results, and Discussion) and stripping all Personally Identifiable Information (PII), the project achieves section-level AI detection benchmarking. In the analysis, AI detection scores for all report sections will be compared across pre-LLM (Large Language Model) and post-LLM cohorts, and used to determine to what extent they moderate any covariation between report grades and exam grades across cohorts.

items.title: AI in Education from CAI to AGI: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping education, yet research remains fragmented across technological streams and often conflates technical capability with demonstrated educational effectiveness. This narrative review synthesizes representative literature published mainly between 2010 and 2026 to trace the evolution of AI-enabled education from computer-assisted instruction toward adaptive, immersive, generative, and potentially more general forms of intelligence. It compares three major technological streams: intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems, extended reality (XR), and large language model-based generative AI. The review finds that intelligent tutoring systems support learner modeling, adaptive feedback, and personalization, but their evidence base is methodologically heterogeneous. XR shows comparatively more consolidated evidence, particularly through systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with generally positive but context-dependent effects on engagement and learning outcomes. Generative AI expands dialogic explanation, scaffolding, content generation, and personalized support, although learner-outcome evidence remains limited relative to capability benchmarking. Building on these findings, the review proposes a Technology–Mechanism–Outcome–Challenge framework and argues that future progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) should be evaluated through learning mechanisms, measurable outcomes, human oversight, equity, and responsible governance.

items.title: AI in the Game Industry: Latest Research Advances and Future Direction
items.abstract: The paper is a summary of the current developments of AI in the gaming sector between 2023 and 2026, including automated generation of content, intelligent game agents (NPCs) and large language models (LLMs), game testing and quality assurance by means of AI, modeling of players and dynamic difficulty management, as well as reorganization of the industry and the new concept of the so-called AI-native games. This study reveals that the use of AI will not be used to assist in the creation of contents but rather become part of the core elements of game mechanics. Real-time diffusion models can model game engines (GameNGen), LLM agents are already implemented in commercial QA systems (TITAN framework), reinforcement learning and player modeling can be applied to adjust the difficulty of the game dynamically based on the data. At the same time, there exists a discussion in the field of efficiency of the process, the creative aspect of it, and how much restructuring of the organization should be done. The authors also suggest some of the criteria which can be used to determine whether a game is an AI-native game (counterfactual testing) and indicate the open issues like automatic playability tests, user acceptance, safety of the contents and ownership of the copyright.

items.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
items.abstract: Abstract Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε). By applying Weaver’s well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

items.abstract: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.

items.title: AI-ASSISTED FINANCIAL JOURNALISM AND THE CREDIBILITY OF CORPORATE FINANCIAL INFORMATION IN NIGERIA
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), including generative AI, natural language processing, machine learning and automated data-analysis systems, is transforming the production and dissemination of financial news. In Nigeria, where journalists increasingly rely on digital tools to interpret corporate disclosures, analyse financial statements and communicate market information to investors and the wider public, AI-assisted financial journalism presents both opportunities and credibility risks. This article examines the relationship between AI-assisted financial journalism and the credibility of corporate financial information in Nigeria. The study adopts an integrative literature-review approach, drawing on recent scholarly literature published between 2024 and 2026. The review is anchored on Source Credibility Theory, Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations Theory, Information Asymmetry Theory and Gatekeeping Theory. Seven recent empirical studies were critically reviewed, including studies of Nigerian journalists' AI adoption, newsroom practices, AI-attributed news credibility, AI disclosure and automated data-driven journalism. The review indicates that AI can improve the speed, analytical capacity, consistency and accessibility of financial journalism, particularly where journalists use AI to process large corporate datasets, identify anomalies, summarise reports and generate preliminary financial stories. However, the credibility benefits are not automatic. Risks arise from hallucinated information, inaccurate numerical interpretation, algorithmic bias, inadequate disclosure, overdependence on automated outputs, weak verification and the cultural and linguistic limitations of AI systems operating in Nigerian contexts. Recent Nigerian evidence also indicates that journalists are increasingly using AI for transcription, editing and preliminary drafting, while human journalists continue to retain important editorial responsibilities. The article argues that the credibility of AI-assisted financial journalism depends less on automation itself than on the quality of human verification, source transparency, professional competence, data provenance and institutional governance surrounding AI use. The article proposes a Human–AI Financial Journalism Credibility Framework in which AI performs computational and assistive functions while journalists retain responsibility for verification, interpretation, contextualisation and ethical publication. The study contributes to emerging literature by connecting AI-assisted journalism with the credibility of corporate financial information in an African emerging-market context.

items.title: AI-based smart waste collection route optimization system
items.abstract: Abstract Efficient collection of solid waste has become a significant challenge in urban areas due to increasing population density and waste generation. Conventional waste collection approach followed a rigid path and time based strategy resulting in heavy utilization of fuel, high operation cost, improper resource utilization, delay in waste collection in critical places. Intelligent data driven waste collection approach is thus required. This paper demonstrates an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based smart waste collection route optimization system combining machine learning based prediction and classical vehicle routing approach. The framework is built to predict the waste bin fill-levels using an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) regressor which identifies bins which require collection. Based on the projected demands for collection a Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) is built and solved using Google OR-Tools to develop an efficient route that is also optimized in terms of fuel utilization while satisfying vehicle capacity constraints. The entire framework is developed using geospatial information data set of 11,058 waste bins and various waste processing facilities provided by Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC). The system is compared using metrics namely, collection distance, fuel consumption and its environmental impact. The current framework overcomes the problem of a reactive traditional system with inefficient prediction by presenting an intelligent and dynamic waste management system, proving that scalable AI-driven route optimization can help in supporting efficient smart city waste management.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Twin Intelligence for Predictive Supply-Chain Resilience and Adaptive Logistics
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being positioned as an intelligence layer for supply-chain systems exposed to uncertain demand, variable lead times, disruptions, energy constraints, and incomplete information. This paper develops a standalone AI-centered framework in which machine-learning prediction, digital-twin synchronization, anomaly detection, resilience assessment, optimization, and operational authorization are treated as distinct but connected functions. The central contribution is an AI decision-admissibility model: an AI prediction is not interpreted as an executable command unless data quality, twin consistency, predictive confidence, operational feasibility, and authorization conditions are simultaneously satisfied. A state-space representation is introduced for demand, inventory, lead time, capacity, energy availability, and disruption risk. Mathematical constructs are developed for predictive error, anomaly intensity, disruption probability, confidence-aware inference, twin consistency, adaptive recovery, explainability, and an AI resilience index. The framework integrates the supplied literature on digital twins, sustainable logistics, AI, blockchain traceability, smart mobility, batteries, electric vehicles, quantum logistics, and supply-chain resilience. A synthetic evaluation structure is proposed so that comparative performance can be studied without fabricating field measurements. The resulting architecture establishes a pathway from telemetry to prediction, validation, optimization, authorization, execution, and learning while retaining human oversight and auditability.

items.title: AI-Driven Drug Repurposing for Multidrug-Resistant Infections: Computational Rigor, Translational Realities, and Strategic Future Directions
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a rapidly escalating global health crisis, and multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacterial pathogens cause substantial morbidity, mortality, and economic burden. Conventional antibiotic-discovery pipelines remain slow, costly, and prone to high attrition, creating an urgent need for alternative strategies. Drug repurposing, which involves identifying new antimicrobial applications for approved or investigational agents, offers a pragmatic and cost-effective approach that leverages existing pharmacokinetic, safety, and formulation data. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and natural language processing (complemented by AI-adjacent computational approaches such as network pharmacology and molecular docking, which are treated here as distinct methods), have accelerated the high-throughput screening and prioritisation of repurposable compounds. This review critically evaluates AI-driven drug repurposing for MDR infections, addressing computational methodologies, data integration, experimental validation, translational bottlenecks, and regulatory considerations. The literature published between January 2020 and September 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, and each case-study drug is annotated for the role of AI and for the level of computational, in vitro, animal, and clinical evidence. We examine methodological limitations, including dataset bias, interpretability constraints, and pharmacokinetic gaps, and highlight the need for explainable AI and rigorous validation frameworks. Case studies of halicin, auranofin, phenothiazines, disulfiram, and clofazimine distinguish agents discovered by AI (halicin) from those whose antimicrobial activity was established by conventional screening or clinical use and illustrate both the promise and the translational hurdles of repurposed antimicrobials. We conclude by outlining strategic pathways for integrating AI predictions with experimental and clinical workflows, emphasising multidisciplinary collaboration to accelerate translation. By combining computational innovation with pharmacological and regulatory rigor, AI-driven repurposing constitutes a complementary strategy to de novo antibiotic discovery, with the potential to expand therapeutic options against MDR pathogens and strengthen global antimicrobial stewardship.
